Survey Summary: Around 10:00 AM PDT on Tuesday, September 2, a
decaying complex of showers and thunderstorms moved over the
Carmichael area in Sacramento County. The National Weather Service
completed a damage survey in coordination with the Sacramento
County Office of Emergency Services. It was determined that the
decaying shower caused a downburst of strong straight-line winds.
Sporadic wind damage to trees and powerlines was noted along with
several mature trees that were uprooted and fell into homes. 
Path length of 2.5 miles. Max path width of 1.5 miles. 0 injuries or fatalities. Surveyed by CC / JW.
Narrow tornado that produced sporadic wind damage along its path with minimal structure damage besides to a few outbuildings.
This short lived tornado damaged crops, a barn, and a tree stand. A pronounced track in fields noted via satellite and UAV photos and a TDS noted on radar.
Initial area of damage from storm, little bit of damage in Callicoon Center with greater amount of damage along J Young rd. Crossed damage path of tornado from April 22, 2023.

Another pocket of damage towards Lawbeach, a few uprooted trees and large branches down. Given that the greatest damage concentration was on hill tops so started the damage path at the top of the ridge in line with the previous area of damage.

The tornado began in a corn field northwest of Mount Sterling with drone footage capturing the swirling corn pattern. The tornado continued southeast damaging a farm outbuilding and several buildings in town before dissipating.
Suspected damage from rear flank downdraft. Damage in this area was rather scattered with debris mostly thrown to the east.

A NWS survey team surveyed damage off of Peak Rd in Pomaria in Newberry County where a strong supercell moved through the evening of November 8th, 2025. The survey found multiple large cedar trees that were either snapped or fully uprooted, mainly facing south or southeast in a divergent pattern. There was also extensive siding damage to the north side of a mobile home from wind-driven hail which was up to golf ball sized. The survey along with radar analysis determined that the wind damage was consistent with a strong downburst within the forward flank downdraft of the supercell with winds up to 85 mph.

An NWS damage survey confirmed that a concentrated area of straight-line wind damage in and west of Forrest was produced by a microburst with estimated peak winds of 80 mph. Damage consisted of downed power poles and trees, at least one shed blown off of its foundation, and a portion of Prairie Central Junior High School's gymnasium roof getting blown off.

Brief tornado touch down on a local maxima in terrain. Caused damage to a couple of small livestock barn and  a small shed was thrown 100 yards left of the track. Another barn in the inflow to the tornado had part of its roof taken off. Some trees fell right near the intersection of Hill Grove and Lickford Bridge.
A tornado damaged the roofs of several homes, destroyed a large outbuilding, and blew down trees.
Roof and siding damage to home and barn heavily damaged.

Montgomery wind damage survey. Winds 60-70 mph in most concentrated area along and near Fairview Ave and Huntingdon College.

Preliminary damage path of the first tornado segment of the Plum Grove Tornado. Tornado appears to initially touched down within a wooded area between CR 3708 and CR 3709, then turned eastward along CR 3709 for a short distance before lifting up shortly before River Ln. Through the use of a drone, did not see any damage in the deeply wooded area along the East Fork of the San Jacinto River. So, will end the first tornado just before the River Ln and CR 3709 intersection.

Majority of the damage seen was broken trunks and branches of pine trees and fences down. Power lines were also reported blown down, but the power line poles remained upright.

The second tornado segment starts along FM 1010 and Wooden Ln with an uprooted tree and broken wood signage. Drone footage showed no signs of damage within the wooded area between the first and second segments. 

The most significant damage occurred at a metal structure off of FM 1010 with preliminary estimated peak winds of 85 mph. The tornado entered a largely empty field between FM 1010 and CR 3405, but still saw some tree damage. The tornado then entered the Bella Vista subdivision, causing tree damage, fence damage, and metal structure damage between CR 3405 and CR 3404. 

No further damage was seen beyond the intersection of CR 3404 and CR 3410.

This tornado developed over heavily wooded, inaccessible (by road) terrain, east of N 161st East Avenue, where the KINX WSR-88D detected a tornadic debris signature. The tornado moved east-northeast across the Caney River, and then destroyed a home and damaged several others south of the river. A large recreational vehicle was rolled and severely damaged. Numerous trees were snapped and outbuildings were damaged. The tornado then moved through another area of inaccessible terrain and crossed the Caney River again, and then crossed the S 4090 Road. Large tree limbs and power poles were snapped as it crossed the E 430 Road, and the tornado dissipated north of the E 430 Road.

Roof and side damage to farm equipment and two chicken houses. About a mile down the road a tobacco barn sustained roof damage. There were scattered small limbs throughout the area. Metal from the buildings was scattered divergently away from the source as they were carried northeast with the wind.

The tornado developed approximately 4 miles northwest of Bristow, west of South 401st West Avenue and north of West 221st Street South. Moving northeast, it crossed South 401st West Avenue, where it destroyed a single-wide mobile home and an outbuilding. As the tornado continued northeast across State Highway 16, it uprooted trees and snapped large limbs. At the intersection of State Highway 48 and West 181st Street South, the tornado impacted an industrial site, collapsing overhead doors and removing roof sections from two metal buildings. The tornado maintained a northeast track, breaking additional tree branches along South 337th West Avenue, before dissipating north of State Highway 66.

This tornado developed just south of the Muskogee Turnpike, east of S 225th East Avenue. It moved northeast across a neighborhood west of S 241st East Avenue, and then into the southern portion of Forest Ridge. The tornado uprooted a few trees, damaged the roofs of several homes, snapped large tree limbs, and blew down large sections of privacy fences.

Chaser video and a debris signature from KINX WSR-88D indicated this tornado began west of highway 48 about 6 miles north-northwest of Castle. The tornado crossed highway 48 where it damaged the roof of two mobile homes and downed small branches along E980 road before dissipating.

This tornado developed over the southern portion of Inola, and moved northeast across the east side of town. One home had a portion of the roof blown off, and a number of other homes received minor damage. Many large limbs were snapped from trees. The tornado then moved northeast across the E 595 Road, where the roof of a home was damaged and trees were blown down. It uprooted trees as it moved across the E 590 Road, crossed Highway 412, and blew a portion of the roof from a home on the E 580 Road. The tornado moved into Mayes County near the E 580 Road, where large tree limbs were snapped and several power poles were blown down. It moved across open country until it dissipated near the W 570 Road and S 427 Road. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D.

This tornado developed just west of N Yale Avenue and north of E 76th Street N. It uprooted a tree as it crossed N Yale Avenue and moved northeast across a neighborhood on E 82nd Street N. Several homes were damaged, light poles were blown down, and large tree limbs were snapped. The tornado blew down power poles and snapped large tree limbs as it crossed E 86th Street N. Outbuildings were damaged and large tree limbs were snapped by the tornado as it crossed N Hudson Avenue, and then crossed N Sheridan Avenue, where it dissipated.

This tornado developed near N Gilcrease Museum Road, north of W Newton Street. It moved northeast damaging a number of homes, damaging the roof of an apartment complex, uprooting trees, and snapping numerous large tree limbs in neighborhoods west of N Tisdale Parkway. It crossed into Tulsa County near W Apache Street. The tornado damaged many homes and snapped numerous large tree limbs between the county line and the Gilcrease Expressway. It continued to move northeast damaging many homes north of the Gilcrease Expressway, and intensified as it approached E 36th Street N. An office building was severely damaged and the Tulsa Technology Center was severely damaged as the tornado approached N Peoria Avenue. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted in that area. The tornado moved north-northeast across E 46th Street N and dissipated north of E 61st Street N. Many homes were damaged, a few trees were uprooted, numerous large tree limbs were snapped, and mobile homes were damaged in that portion of the path. This tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D.

The tornado began on the west side of Beggs, directly impacting the Beggs Public Schools campus.
The High School and Middle School roof sustained significant damage, and the bus barn was also suffered heavy damage to the roof and overhead doors. As it moved northeast, it crossed 15th Street, uprooting and snapping trees. After crossing Happy Camp Road, it destroyed outbuildings and began a brief jog northward, paralleling North 180 Rd. This strongest and widest phase of the tornado occurred as it moved east along Grimes Road. One single-wide manufactured home was completely destroyed and several other single-family residences were heavily damaged with the loss of roofs and windows. Two fatalities and two injuries occurred at one homestead where a double-wide manufactured home was completely destroyed and several automobiles were moved and tossed 20–30 yards. A nearby barn was destroyed and heavy limb loss occurred on large trees. The tornado then continued northeast crossing State Highway 75, where it threw a metal shipping container across the lanes and uprooted trees. The tornado dissipated after crossing North 205 Road about three miles south of the Tulsa County line.

A microburst, combined with large hail, moved for at least 15 miles (based on survey points) across southern Starr County, Texas, between 1126 PM CST March 8 and 1204 AM CST March 9th. Wind speeds generally ranged from 65 to 70 mph based on damage indicators, degree of damage, and fair to poor construction of damaged elements.  At least 100 windows were shattered by the wind driven hail in one neighborhood, 2.5 miles northwest of the center of Rio Grande City. At least 8 homes surveyed lost up to 20% of shingles down to the roof decking, with the combination of wind and hail damaging at least two dozen roofs with lesser shingle damage.

An Exxon service station in east Rio Grande City had its canopy flipped when the winds got underneath it and tore at poorly anchored poles.  A poorly built structure (not part of this survey) on Zinnia Street west of the Starr County/Rio Grande City Airport was destroyed by the gusts.

Hail size in the surveyed damage area in Rio Grande City ranged from quarter to at least golfball-sized. Lesser hail size was noted in Roma by Fire Department personnel.

A rear-flank downdraft caused extensive wind damage across Havana, primarily north of US-136. Numerous trees were damaged, and some buildings sustained damage as well. Wind gusts were estimated to be 80 to 90 mph.
EF0 damage area

A large swath of wind damage occurred at the end of the tornado path to the east and south/southeast. Much of this was in and to the south side of the town of Bassfield. The worst damage from this wind swath was south of town along Bassfield Cemetery road where numerous trees were uprooted or damaged along with power lines down and sheds damaged and some homes damaged due to trees on them. Estimated peak winds were 85 mph.
EF0 wind/damage area

The National Weather Service conducted a storm damage survey in Gaffney, SC. It was determined that damage was caused by straight-line winds peaking around 75 mph. These damaging winds were from a line of severe thunderstorms that moved through Northeast Georgia, Western North Carolina, and the South Carolina Upstate Monday morning.



Damage was first observed within the city limits, where corrugated metal roof panels, wooden joists, and fascia were ripped off the front of a small business along West Frederick Street (Route 11). The wind also shifted the exterior metal wall of a nearby auto parts store, causing the corner panels to buckle and separate. Approximately one-third mile east, a large tree was uprooted next to a house between Marion Avenue and Mill Street.



Based on radar analysis, as well as the fact that the damage was sporadic and lacked any signs of circulation, it was determined the damage was caused by a localized downburst of straight-line winds rather than a tornado.
A swath of winds developed along the southern path of the Bass Burkett Tornado. Downed trees were noted from Greens Creek road through Highway 35. Peak winds were 65-75 mph.
A swath of damaging winds occurred east of Bassfield, generally between two other tornado paths. Here peak winds were between 65-75 mph and multiple trees were damaged or blown down.

Between corridors of tornadic wind damage, a swath of straightline wind damage associated with a line of severe thunderstorms spread from near Ruth in Lincoln County to the north side of Jayess in Lawrence County. Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped, and some fell onto sheds, homes, and power lines. Estimated peak winds were 90 mph. Path length was 8 miles and around 2.6 miles wide at its widest.

The tornado begin 2 miles NNE of Hillsboro, continuing northeast for about 7 miles. The worst damage, rated lower EF3 with winds to 140 mph, was to a home on Raese Road NW of Union Center. A large downburst interacted with the tornado downstream of this point as the tornado tracked north and northeast of Union Center with the width of the downburst nearly 1/2 of a mile in spots. After the tornado crossed the Baraboo River, the downburst began undercutting the tornado and eventually caused the circulation to dissipate near Ackerman Road. There was one brief spin-up from the parent mesocyclone about a mile downstream of this point which has been included in the path of the main tornado.

What was likely rear flank downdraft (RFD) winds and a strong dust whirl or gustnado on this wind surge based on three videos. The damage was a destroyed old grain bin and three outbuilding roofs, branches snapped, a tree downed, and to the press box at the soccer field at the high school.

A swath of strong straight-line winds affected southeast Trumbull County in Brookfield Township. Damage was observed along Everett East Road from west of County Route 167 to Greensleaves Circle.

Along Everett East Road, winds lifted a trampoline from a backyard, deposited it in a residence's front yard, and blew down a fence. In the Trumbull County Metroparks, on the north side of Everett East Road, approximately 30 to 40 trees were blown down, all oriented toward the southeast. Several healthy trees were snapped at the base of the trunk, supporting higher-end wind estimates.

A large tree was also blown down on the north side of Everett East Road, clipping a home and damaging the roof. Additionally, several large tree limbs fell onto two homes, causing minor structural damage. Other trees were downed on the south side of Everett East Road.

All observed tree damage and debris were consistently oriented toward the southeast, indicating straight-line wind damage. Maximum wind gusts are estimated at about 90 mph.

We appreciate the Brookfield Fire Department's assistance with this survey.

This tornado developed northwest of Saratoga and tracked northeast, damaging one outbuilding during its existence. The tornado was witnessed and photographed by multiple individuals. The tornado rolled a truck, with the driver suffering minor injuries.

This EF0 tornado began near the Dodge and Mower County line before entering rural Dodge County. The tornado caused minor damage to a grain silo and downed several trees. The track continued northeast and weakened/roped out. This tornado was captured in video from MNDOT cameras south of Rochester.

This EF0 tornado affected mainly rural areas southeast of Oslo MN and was on the ground concurrently with another tornado to the west for several minutes. Mainly farm outbuildings and trees sustained light damage along the path of the tornado.

Appears to be from downburst winds as most damage appears to be pushed down with no signs of lofted debris. The hardest hit area was in the Forest Subdivision west of Veteran's Memorial Park.  This area sits at a higher elevation and it looks like the wind caught a lot of pine trees and either uprooted or snapped them.  The two buildings that had direct wind damage to them were the Milwaukee Valve facility and a Sanitation building.  The Sanitation building had it's north wall blown in, but none of the roofing material.  For the Valve building, it appears that the corner of a roof peeled back with some of the insulation blowing onto the apartment complex to the southeast.  This is the only material that was seen 'lofted' but it's possible that due to the higher level of the building that the insulation just blew sideways.  Radar also is inconclusive for any sort of rotation or debris signature.

A large area of wind damage occurred in far southern Schuyler County, mainly west of Beardstown. Much of it was concentrated along state highway 103. Widespread wind gusts of 80 to 100 mph caused significant tree damage, and a farm was severely hit near the intersection of Cottonwood Rd. and Downing Rd. The farm owner confirmed the damage occurrred during the late afternoon storm, rather than the line of storms that arrived a couple hours later.

The tornado formed on the northeast of Stewartville and traveled about 10 miles north-northeast, damaging numerous homes and farms. Some of the worst damage was seen near Marion Road, just northeast of Highway 52, where multiple homes were severely damaged with roof removal and partially collapsed exterior walls.

This tornado developed southwest of Hatfield along the Black River and churned eastward, causing extensive damage to trees as it roughly paralleled Old Highway 54. Despite the extensive tree damage, damage to buildings along the path was limited. The tornado was embedded within a larger downburst that caused equal, if not greater, damage than the tornado itself. The downburst undercut the tornado after only a few minutes in existence.

A broad area of straight line wind damage or an embedded microburst developed 1-2 miles to the south and southeast of an EF1 tornado. At least 30-40 power poles were either snapped near their base or leaning. One of the buildings at the Cortland Egg Farms sustained significant uplift of its aluminum roof. Multiple trees and limbs were downed  along Co Road 800N as well.

Destructive straight line winds impacted southeast parts of Ripley County, Missouri, on the afternoon of Tuesday, April 28, 2026. The damage swath began just southeast of Doniphan, where a home suffered roof, siding, and fascia damage. 

Moving east-southeast, damaging wind impacted the Oxly community and location near and south of the Naylor community. In Oxly, dozens of trees were snapped or uprooted, causing damage to outbuildings and downing power lines. To the south and west of Naylor, a grain bin will rolled hundreds of yards and a large farm outbuilding was shifted off its foundation. 

Along the damage path, hundreds of trees were snapped, uprooted, or lost large limbs. A few power poles were broken as well.

This tornado developed several miles southwest of Cream and reached its peak intensity quickly as it descended a ridge to the west of State Road 88, where low-end EF3 damage was observed to one house. The tornado tracked onward to the northeast and damaged mostly trees and a few residences along the remainder of its path as a high end EF1.
Microburst confirmed by storm survey team.

Survey teams found substantial wind damage to trees and a few
structures in the community of Piggott. Tree damage was relatively widespread, with numerous uprooted and downed trees. Minor structural damage and a few downed utility lines were also noted. The damage swath was approximately one mile wide, mainly affecting the northern side of town, with trees and debris blown to the southeast, consistent with an intense rear flank downdraft. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at around 80 mph.

A sizeable swath of wind damage developed across south-central Jasper county and moved into northeast Jones during the afternoon o April 29th. Much of this wind was in the 60-65 mph range. However, a more intense corridor developed on the east side of the Moss community and in the Bonner community with peak winds between 70-80 mph. Numerous trees were damaged from being uprooted, snapped, or had large limbs broken off. These were downed in a south facing direction. Three homes had trees down on them along with some on a couple sheds. Power lines and poles were downed by trees as well. Worst impacted areas were along CR 31, 33, 311 in Jasper Co and the 400-500 blocks of Claiborne road and Bonner road in NE Jones Co.

A supercell storm moved out of Drew county near the Jerome community and produced a swath of winds of 70-80 mph across central Chicot Co into and around Lake Village. Power lines and poles were down in the rural parts of the county. Most of the damage in Lake Village was around Mulberry Street. Here multiple trees were uprooted across a few block radius. Power lines were down as well.

A potent mid-level disturbance developed a few evenly spaced strong 
to severe storms over south-central Texas, that moved southeastward 
into the Victoria Crossroads region (Live Oak to Refugio counties 
eastward). Although these storms developed in the wake of the 
surface cold front, they interacted with each other, likely 
enhancing the northernmost storm's intensity through a phenomena 
called GWAC (Gravity Wave Associated Convection).

The northernmost storm developed a well-defined rear flank downdraft 
(RFD) gust front as it entered north-central Goliad County around 
1:15pm CDT. The storm intensified with a bowing segment along the 
RFD highlighted by strong reflectivity around the Coleto Creek 
Reservoir, where the first damage of RVs rolled over were reported 
shortly after 1:50pm CDT. Soon after, the rear inflow jet descended 
to the surface and produced 60-90 mph winds near the intersection of 
HWY-59 and HWY-77; large branches broke with power poles leaning. 

Further intensification was evident later on between 2:00-2:20pm CDT 
along and between HWY-185 to HWY-87 including the cities of Dernal, 
Guadalupe, Dacosta, and Placedo. This is where the greatest damage 
was observed; many manufactured homes suffered from significant roof 
damage, windows blown out, and some walls collapsed. In addition, 
numerous large tree branches were broken, trees uprooted, and 
numerous power poles leaned or were completely snapped/broken.

The dangerously strong winds continued east-southeast into northern 
Matagorda Bay, where less friction and obstruction amplified winds to 
100-120 mph into Point Comfort from 2:30-2:35pm CDT. Around 33 power 
poles and 4 double pole transmission lines were damaged in Point 
Comfort, aligning with the 119 mph wind gust observed at a 
Weatherflow HurrNet site. Another mesonet station nearby measured a 
wind gust to 98 mph and a third station recorded a gust of ~114 mph 
(when accounting for friction, since the actual measurement was 180 
feet AGL). A few manufactured homes exposed closest to the bay 
suffered significant roof and wall damage.

Evidence of a high-end EF-1 (110mph) tornado was found in south-
central Victoria County. Drone footage showed a scour track that 
began over farmland between Crouch Rd and HWY-185, and ended near 
Crouch Rd east of York Rd along with a track of debris. In between, 
several manufactured homes on Jared Rd, Lexie Ln, and York Rd 
suffered significant roof damage, broken windows, and scattered 
debris correlated to circulation of a tornado. One manufactured home 
was completely destroyed along Jared Rd. The tornado track was found 
to be around 1.1 miles long and a width of around 400 yards, 
spanning from 2:02-2:06pm CDT.

Surveyed wind damage began in south Harlingen at the intersection of Camelot Road/Ed Carey and Interstate 69E, and continued through San Benito (mainly the east and south portion), before the event (wet microburst) produced the most visible damage from Green Valley Farms through Laureles in central Cameron County. The surveyed path length was approximately 13.5 miles, an the path width generally ranged from 1 to just under 3 miles. Wind speeds ranged from 65 to 80 mph on the survey track; a Texas Mesonet location about 1 miles southeast of Green Valley Farms recorded an instantaneous gust of 82 mph, which fits closely with estimated wind speeds at points along Iowa Gardens Road. 

Unfortunately, there were three known significant injuries, two at a residence along Chappell Road in Green Valley Farms, and one along Country Boy Road in east San Benito. 

The most pronounced damage was to poorly built/unanchored single-wide manufactured or mobile trailer-type structures, as well as RVs, in Green Valley Farms - an area of colonias between San Benito and Los Fresnos. Additional damage was noted in the town of Laureles, where shingle and some decking was lifted from roofs of somewhat better construction.  A large but aged wooden billboard (about 80 feet AGL) at the intersection of Interstate 69E and Business 77 in south San Benito (Exit 17) blew down.  

Hundreds of trees, including mesquite, ash, and live oak, were impacted - from large limbs snapped near the trunks to smaller (1-3" limbs) snapped off.  

The survey team conducted interviews of impacted residents to see how they were faring, but also to ask them for descriptions of the event as it passed.  The survey, these descriptions, radar interrogation, and dozens of photos and videos clearly confirmed a fast-moving west-to-east wet microburst caused the damage.

A storm exhibiting supercell characteristics for multiple hours while offshore moved ashore with a tornado estimated to have touched down around 1814 UTC (2:14 PM EDT) west of U.S. Hwy 19 near Hudson in Pasco County, while continuing to exhibit a distinct rotational signature via KTBW WSR-88D and TTPA TDWR. Damage was initially observed along Saltwater Blvd, where a tree branch was snapped and fell onto a power line. Additional damage points were noted to manufactured homes further east along Saltwater Blvd -- one having its rear screened porch lifted from its base attachment and partially shifted, along with metal roofing peeled and tossed across the street, and another suffering partial roof loss with metal roofing above its garage lifted and peeled off. Additional damage was noted north of Saltwater Blvd, with a family residence along Neptune Drive having approximately five to ten feet of fascia peeled off the side of the home near the roof. Neighboring manufactured homes located approximately a quarter-mile to the east along Puffin Lane experienced rear porch roof and lanai damage, with one home losing part of its aluminum roof as it was peeled from the back of the home and lofted over the home and into a vehicle parked in its front yard, and also onto the street in front of the home. The neighboring home just to its east had its rear lanai peeled from the home and tossed around it onto a metal fence across the street from the home. Along the adjacent Osprey Lane to the north, a large pine tree had its top snapped off, and a small wooden outdoor shed was collapsed, while on adjacent Heron and Curlew Lanes to the north, homes suffered partial carport aluminum panel loss and partial aluminum roofing material loss, respectively. The final damage point noted west of U.S. Hwy 19 consisted of small to medium sized branches snapped and broken from trees near the intersection of Gull Lane and Delmar Drive. The tornado then crossed U.S. Hwy 19 with the radar signature becoming increasingly disorganized shortly thereafter, and it is estimated that the tornado dissipated sometime around 1819 UTC (2:19 PM EDT) between Whitby Road and Lakeshore Blvd after tracking for just over one mile.

The development of a second circulation became apparent west of Shady Hills around 20 minutes after the circulation associated with the Hudson tornado weakened, and it is estimated that a tornado touched down near Gladwin Avenue to the west of East Road at approximately 1843 UTC (2:43 PM EDT). Damage from this tornado consisted largely of snapped tree limbs and branches as it slowly tracked south and southeast across largely rural areas along Fulton and Eden Avenue, although a large tree was uprooted and downed onto a mobile home along Eden Avenue near the intersection of East Road. The tornado then turned east and east-southeast as it appeared to exhibit a bit of a binary interaction with the remnant circulation that produced the Hudson tornado that was located to its east, before radar indicated it likely dissipated around 1848 UTC (2:48 PM EDT) between East Road and Alliance Lane, less than mile from where it is estimated to have touched down.

A landspout tornado likely associated with the circulation responsible for a previous landspout is estimated to have formed around 3:25 PM EDT approximately 1.75 miles to the northwest of the previous landspout, where damage was first noted along Reynard Ave in the Tanglewood area where a large tree had numerous medium to large branches snapped. Branches and limbs were snapped at multiple locations across Cumberland and Woodwind Courts, and a home near Tanglewood Pkwy had a large tree uprooted in its yard. Additional footage was submitted from the Tanglewood vicinity depicting lawn furniture and yard decor scattered about, along with fencing and roof damage, and a video taken by a resident along Westminster Dr at 3:28 PM EDT showed airborne debris along with indications of the ground circulation as the landspout neared the McGregor Gardens area and Argyle Dr and McGregor Blvd. The circulation continued northwest across the Georgetown area just south of Colonial Blvd and began crossing the Caloosahatchee River just to the west-southwest of McGregor Colonial Memorial Park, and to the south of the Midpoint Bridge around 3:30 PM EDT. Videos taken by the public showed surface spray associated with the circulation as it approached and crossed the Midpoint Bridge west of McGregor Colonial Memorial Park and continued northwest toward the central section of the river north of the bridge, where it is estimated to have dissipated sometime around 3:31 PM EDT before reaching the western shore of the river.

The downdraft region of an intense supercell thunderstorm produced a swath of widespread 70 to 95 mph winds. The wind damage was particularly noteworthy and extensive in the town of Auburn where very large branches or trees were snapped or uprooted in almost every block of the town. Many of these trees were weaker silver maples, but even some stronger oaks sustained significant damage. Structural damage was limited, but there was one old brick building in the downtown area that suffered a roof failure that then allowed walls to collapse. This area of downdraft winds was several miles wide and several miles long, and there was also evidence that some 60-80 mph winds extended all the way back toward Elk Creek and Tecumseh.

A landspout tornado formed over Cape Coral just north of the Sovereign Canal around 3:35 PM EDT in association with a separate segment of the cluster of thunderstorms, with evidence of the circulation visible in video taken by residents along SW 4th Ave and SW 5th Ave. Footage from SW 4th Ave showed a pickup truck in the driveway of a home being displaced a number of feet as the circulation passed by the location, and footage from the SW 5th Ave location showed the funnel of the landspout and the surface circulation behind a home over the Niagara Canal. Additional footage of the circulation was taken approximately one-quarter mile to the northwest near the Seabell Canal, where footage from a home on the southern edge of the canal along SW 26th Ter showed the circulation blowing lawn chairs around and lofting additional unidentified debris, while also knocking over and blowing around vinyl fencing in the backyard of a home on the opposite/northern side of the canal along SW 26th St. A few additional reports and photos from the vicinity also indicated fence and some roof damage as the circulation neared the intersection of Skyline Blvd and Veterans Pkwy before before it is estimated to have dissipated around 3:38 PM EDT, as no other reports, pictures or videos have been confirmed to indicate that the track extended further.

A landspout tornado was observed at 3:17 PM EDT just to the east of U.S. Hwy 41/S Cleveland Ave and north of Woodland Blvd, where a citizen submitted video of a rotating cloud base and funnel near the Wawa and Culvers, and later confirmed that they witnessed a ground circulation with surface and lofted dust and small debris. No significant damage was reported, and no other reports, pictures or videos have been received indicating that the track extended beyond that location.

The National Weather Service Cleveland conducted a storm damage survey in cooperation with the Lorain County Emergency Management Agency following severe thunderstorms that moved through Lorain County on the evening of Wednesday, June 10, 2026. The survey determined that two separate microbursts produced significant straight-line wind damage across the City of Amherst between approximately 8:23 PM and 8:30 PM EDT.

The first microburst occurred around 8:23 PM and affected portions of central Amherst near Cleveland Avenue and areas just west of South Leavitt Road. Damage included siding torn from a building along Cleveland Avenue, two large trees uprooted along Cleveland Avenue, and several large tree limbs falling onto a detached garage west of South Leavitt Road. In addition, more than 30 large tree limbs were snapped or broken throughout the damaged path. The damage pattern was consistent with divergent winds associated with a microburst.

A second microburst occurred around 8:30 PM in the northeastern portion of Amherst. The most concentrated damage was observed north of State Route 2 and near North Ridge Road, including the Cooper Foster Park Road West corridor. Thunderstorm wind gusts overturned a storage container, snapped a utility pole, and knocked down a restaurant sign along Cooper Foster Park Road West. Two large trees were uprooted and fell across Cooper Foster Park Road West, and an additional seven trees were uprooted in the surrounding area. Approximately 50 tree limbs were also downed onto power lines, homes, and roadways. As with the first area of damage, an additional seven trees were uprooted in the surrounding area. Approximately 50 tree limbs were also downed onto power lines, homes, and roadways. As with the first area of damage, the observed pattern was consistent with a microburst producing strong divergent winds.

Based on the extent and severity of the damage observed during the survey, peak wind speeds were estimated at up to 85 mph in the strongest portions of the microbursts. The National Weather Service Cleveland extends its appreciation to the Lorain County EMA for providing transportation assistance and participating in the storm survey. Their support was instrumental in documenting the damage and completing the assessment.

An EF1 Tornado hit Rock Stream, NY, crossed Seneca Lake and hit lakeshore residence south of Hector, NY during late morning on June 18, 2026. Though there was pockets of minor tree damage from the storm itself, tornadic damage started around Reading Road at 1045 AM. This tornado strengthened to as much as 90 mph from Old Lake Road to State Route 14, as rotation tightened with the storm quickly moving at 50 mph from higher elevations into the Seneca Lake basin. Numerous trees were uprooted in a convergent chaotic fashion, and around 40 vineyard posts were snapped. Twigs and branches were impaled into the ground as missiles in portions of the vineyard, and shingles were found more than a quarter mile from their source. A garage outbuilding collapsed, with some metal roof peelback and siding damage also noted on the residence with small branches squeezing into gaps. After crossing State Route 14 with a continued corridor of uprooted trees, the tornado crossed Seneca Lake around 1050 AM. Significant damage was observed near the lake at the end of Wickham Rd. A large tree branch was impaled into a house and several trees and numerous large branches were downed.

An EF-0 tornado briefly touched down 3.4 miles west of Cortland in Cortland County NY around 11:32 AM, moving east-northeast at 50 mph. Tree damage along the route was the most common type of damage, with a swath of tree damage showing a convergent pattern, which is indication of a brief tornado touching down. Going east along Route 222, and along residential streets south of Route 222, multiple trees fell in the east-northeast direction, with a few falling due north. Where convergent damage was evident was just north of the Cortland County Airport, with a few trees falling in the southwest direction. Among the damage, some of the most extensive was mainly large uprooted trees and large snapped trees. Going further east-northeast, further scattered tree damage was observed, but did not show a convergent pattern. This indicated that the brief tornado dissipated heading into town, and was residual thunderstorm wind damage.

Shortly after 4:00 pm a microburst occurred beneath a mesocyclone in a broken line of thunderstorms crossing Lake Winnipesaukee. Areal extent of damage was likely larger owing to the lack of friction over the lake itself. Damage was reported and/or surveyed on Round, Welch, Sandy, Ragged, and Cow Islands, where the damage was particularly intense. An estimated 1500 trees were snapped or uprooted, particularly on Cow Island. There were at least 6 camps that sustained damage due to falling trees, as well as at least 2 docks that were damaged. Precise areal measurements are difficult with a lack of damage indicators over water, but the path length and width were roughly 3 miles by 0.75 miles respectively.

A second microburst developed beneath the same mesocyclone in the broken line of thunderstorms. This one occurred between 4:10 pm and 4:15 pm. About a half mile wide and three quarters of a mile long, this microburst was a little more intense than the first, with winds up to 100 mph. An estimate of at least 1500 trees were snapped or uprooted in this area. In addition 5 vehicles were damaged, 2 of which were totaled. There were 5 cabins or outbuildings that were destroyed, and another 12 that were damaged to varying degrees. All of these were the result of tree falls.

A combination of a storm survey, eyewitness reports, and radar data indicates that damage from a severe storm across western Wheeler was caused by a strong rear-flank downdraft on the backside of a powerful supercell. The path of the most significant damage was approximately one mile wide. The most severe damage occurred in an RV park, where 16 unanchored travel trailers were rolled and destroyed. The south end of the trailer park was downstream from open areas, which likely contributed to higher wind speeds and greater damage in that specific section of the park. One injury was reported, but most residents had either evacuated to a shelter or were not home at the time. An overturned pickup truck at the site was likely pushed over by adjacent rolling trailers. Other damage included snapped power poles, numerous broken large tree limbs, and a few uprooted trees. Several homes and businesses sustained significant roof damage, including metal buildings that were compromised after their overhead doors failed. Most well-constructed or newer structures sustained only minor damage or remained unscathed. Peak wind speeds are estimated to have been near 100 mph.

Around midnight on 6 August 2026, a cluster of severe thunderstorms advancing into Cass County developed severe outflow winds in excess of 70 to 80 mph, with pockets of significantly severe, 90 to 100 mph, wind gusts across northwestern Cass County Missouri, from Belton to Raymore, and into southern Jackson County, impacting neighborhoods in far south Lee’s Summit. As two separate thunderstorms merged moving into Cass County, with significant influence from the low level jet stream, a swath of severe outflow winds developed near I-49/US 71 in northern Belton, increasing in intensity as the storm surged across northern Raymore over the Creekmore Neighborhood. Radar analysis found divergent downburst signatures indicative of widespread 80+ mph wind gusts with pockets of radial downburst signatures suggesting wind speeds approaching 90 to 100 mph along the Cass/Jackson border from Creekmore, in Raymore, to Stony Creek in Lee’s Summit. NWS Damage survey confirmed widespread 70 to 80 mph wind damage, primarily to trees and unsecured items, within a wide swath along the damage path, with pockets of 80 to 90 mph damage to trees and structures. Early in the event, significant damage was noted west of I-49/US 71 to a distribution warehouse where a prefabricated concrete wall failed. The most significant damage was found just east-northeast of Creekmore, where large trees were toppled and significant damage occurred to a steel frame constructed equestrian show barn. Wind speeds were estimated to be between 95 and 100 mph based on the damage to trees and the equestrian barn. The survey found additional damage to trees and minor structure damage into the Stony Creek and Rain Tree Lake neighborhoods of south Lee’s Summit.

An intense thunderstorm produced extensive straightline wind damage across portions of Morristown on Saturday afternoon, August 8th. The first noted damage was minor tree damage along Clearview Road and Central Church Road near Joe Stephens. As the storm collapsed the winds were maximized in a corridor along Central Church Road near Antioch Road, Tennessee Hills Drive, and Grove Dale Drive. Here large swaths of trees were uprooted and blown down primarily to the east and southeast. Some homes sustained moderate to significant damage when trees fell on or through the homes in this area. Preliminary estimates indicated that up to 10 homes may have been damaged in this area. A few power poles were also observed to be snapped or damaged. The maximum estimated winds were also observed in this general location and was estimated to be around 80 mph. The collapsing phase of the storm was finally complete with sporadic tree damage noted on the west side of the country club and near McBride Road and Catron Lane.

Around 6 AM CDT on Wednesday, 5 August 2026, a cluster of severe thunderstorms along the Iowa/Missouri border moved into a more favorable environment for damaging outflow and downburst wind development. Through 6:15 AM CDT, the southern storm began to develop a bowing segment as it traversed east across Mercer County Missouri. As the storm crossed near Ravanna, MO it developed widespread 60 to 70 mph winds. Significant damage was noted to a commercial hog barn in eastern Mercer County with noted sporadic tree damage along the US 136 Corridor into Putnam  County. Around 6:40 AM CDT, east of Lucerne, the roof to a home was lifted off, estimated 90 mph downburst winds accelerated along an open fetch of land up to the home on the hill top. All debris from the home was deposited to the east, with no convergent damage pattern found or wind blown debris or mud splatter back to the north or west on the home. About three quarters of a mile north, an outbuilding was also blown down and debris spread east. Following the storms path through 7 AM toward and through Unionville, sporadic 65 to 75 mph tree damage was noted along with minor structure damage to farm outbuildings. Within Unionville, widespread 65 to 75 mph tree damage was noted along with minor roof damage to buildings along the downtown square. Estimate overall swath of wind damage to be about 25 miles long and 2 to 3 miles wide.

A series of severe downbursts caused intermittent damage to trees and agricultural fields, snapped power poles, damaged at least one home, and blew the roof off of one barn. The maximum damage intensity appears to be in line with winds estimated at 90 mph, and extended from an area approximately 3 miles north northwest of Dodge through the far southern side of West Point. There were additional reports of damage east of West Point. While the peak damage intensity areas were intermittent, there were no clearly identifiable signs of focused rotation tracks within the broader downburst area. Numerous cornfields were impacted, and the corn damage was all pointing in the same southwest-to-northeast direction and sporadically spread across significant widths of the field. Tree branches also blew in that direction (southwest to northeast). The severe downburst damage was at times up to 4 miles wide.

A waterspout developed from a shower just offshore of Folly Beach, SC near the Washout area around 1235 PM. The waterspout moved slowly west-northwest before coming onshore as a tornado around 1236 PM, near the Fort and East Ashley Avenue intersection at the Washout. The tornado moved across the beach, throwing a few tents/umbrellas, chairs, surfboards and beach coverings into the air before dissipating just beyond East Ashley Avenue approximately 30 seconds after reaching land. Damage was minimal, with only minor impacts seen on video at the beach given a lack of vegetation and structures in the vicinity. Despite the tornado moving directly over a group of people, no injuries have been reported. Based on public video footage and the lack of damage indicators, the tornado is rated EF0 with maximum winds estimated to be near 55 mph. Tornado width approximately 15 yards.
